title: Quantization & Oversampling
description: Model A/D and D/A converters as DSP blocks: quantization noise, SQNR, oversampling, noise shaping and anti-aliasing requirements.

study.title: A/D and D/A as DSP blocks
study.body: A DSP system sees the analog world through two converters. The **A/D** path is an anti-aliasing low-pass filter, a sampler (C/D) and a **quantizer**; the **D/A** path holds each sample for one period $T$ and smooths the resulting staircase. We treat the sampler as ideal and lump every imperfection of the A/D into one additive error: the quantization noise. Notation as in O&S: $\Omega$ is analog frequency in rad/s, $\omega = \Omega T$ discrete-time frequency in rad/sample. Careful: the Discrete-Time Signals & Systems subject (Phillips) used the letters the other way round, $\Omega$ for discrete time and $\omega$ for analog frequency.

study.title: Explore: the uniform quantizer
study.body: A $B$-bit quantizer has $2^B$ levels spread over the full-scale range $-X_m \ldots X_m$, so the step is $\Delta = 2X_m/2^B$. A **rounding** quantizer picks the nearest level, so the error stays within $\pm\Delta/2$ as long as the input is in range; above $X_m - \Delta/2$ it clips and the error grows. Drag $B$: every extra bit halves $\Delta$. (O&S counts $B + 1$ bits, a sign bit plus $B$; here $B$ is the total.)

study.title: The additive noise model
study.body: For a busy signal that crosses many levels, the error $e[n] = Q(x[n]) - x[n]$ behaves like random noise: **uniformly distributed** between $-\Delta/2$ and $\Delta/2$, **white** (uncorrelated from sample to sample) and **uncorrelated with the signal**. The quantizer then acts as an adder, $\hat{x}[n] = x[n] + e[n]$. A uniform density of width $\Delta$ has zero mean and variance $\Delta^2/12$. The model fails for constant or very small inputs, where the error simply follows the signal.

study.title: Signal-to-quantization-noise ratio
study.body: $\mathrm{SQNR} = 10\log_{10}(\sigma_x^2/\sigma_e^2)$. Substituting $\sigma_e^2$ gives the rule below: **6.02 dB per bit**, minus the headroom between the range $X_m$ and the signal's rms value $\sigma_x$. A full-scale sine ($\sigma_x = X_m/\sqrt{2}$) gets $6.02B + 1.76$ dB. Example: 12 bits, $\pm$2.5 V range, a sine of 1 V amplitude: $6.02 \cdot 12 + 1.76 - 20\log_{10}(2.5/1)$ = 74.0 − 8.0 = 66.0 dB. A Gaussian signal needs $X_m \approx 4\sigma_x$ to avoid clipping and gets $6.02B - 7.3$ dB.

study.title: D/A conversion and the zero-order hold
study.body: A D/A converter holds each sample for one period $T$, so its output is a staircase: the samples convolved with a rectangular pulse. That pulse has a sinc-shaped frequency response with nulls at multiples of $f_s$. It weakens the spectral images, but it also **droops** inside the signal band, by 3.92 dB at $f_s/2$. The analog smoothing filter removes what is left of the images; the droop is equalised with an $x/\sin x$ boost, digitally or in the analog filter.

study.title: Oversampling
study.body: White quantization noise spreads its power $\sigma_e^2$ evenly over $0 \ldots f_s/2$. If the signal only occupies $0 \ldots f_B$ and we sample at $f_s = 2Mf_B$, a digital low-pass filter (followed by decimation) keeps only $1/M$ of the noise. Each doubling of the **oversampling ratio** $M$ gains 3 dB, half a bit, so one extra bit costs a factor 4 in sampling rate. A bonus: the analog anti-aliasing filter gets a wide transition band.

study.title: Explore: noise shaping
study.body: A **sigma-delta** (ΣΔ) modulator puts the quantizer in a feedback loop with an integrator. The signal passes unchanged, but the quantization error leaves through the high-pass $1 - z^{-1}$: its spectrum is pushed **out of the signal band**, where the decimation filter removes it. With first-order shaping the in-band noise falls as $1/M^3$, 9 dB per doubling of $M$ (1.5 bits); an order-$L$ loop gives $(2L+1) \cdot 3$ dB per doubling. Drag $M$ and compare the noise left in the band $0 \ldots \pi/M$ (relative to $\sigma_e^2$).

study.title: Anti-aliasing filter requirements
study.body: Everything that would alias **into the signal band** must be attenuated below the noise floor, roughly by the SQNR, before the sampler. A tone at $f$ aliases to $|f - kf_s|$, which lands in $0 \ldots f_B$ only if $f > f_s - f_B$. When a digital filter removes $f_B \ldots f_s/2$ afterwards, the analog filter may use all of $f_B \ldots f_s - f_B$ as transition band. An order-$N$ Butterworth with its −3 dB point at $f_B$ gives about $20N\log_{10}(f/f_B)$ dB well above $f_B$. Example, $f_B$ = 20 kHz and 96 dB: at $f_s$ = 48 kHz (alias edge 28 kHz) this takes $N$ = 33; at 64× oversampling ($f_s$ = 2.56 MHz) $N$ = 3 is enough.

steps.title: Converters as DSP blocks
steps.body: Every DSP system that touches the real world has an **A/D** converter at its input and a **D/A** converter at its output. Here we treat them as signal-processing blocks: the A/D samples and **quantizes**, the D/A **holds** and smooths. Notation follows O&S: $\omega$ is the discrete-time frequency in rad/sample, $\Omega$ the analog frequency in rad/s, and $\omega = \Omega T$. That swaps the letters of the Discrete-Time Signals & Systems subject, which used $\Omega$ for discrete time.

steps.prompt: Put the blocks of a DSP system in signal order, from analog input to analog output.
steps.explanation: The anti-aliasing filter must act **before** sampling: once a component has aliased, no digital filter can tell it apart from a genuine in-band signal. Sampler and quantizer together form the A/D. After processing, the D/A holds each sample (a staircase) and the analog smoothing filter removes the spectral images around multiples of $f_s$.

steps.title: The uniform quantizer
steps.body: A $B$-bit converter has $2^B$ output levels across its full-scale range $-X_m \ldots X_m$, so the step is $\Delta = 2X_m/2^B$. Rounding to the nearest level gives an error of at most $\Delta/2$ while the input stays in range. Drag $B$ to see the staircase and its error.

steps.prompt: A {{B}}-bit A/D converter has a full-scale range of $\pm${{Xm|V}}.

ask.prompt: What is the largest rounding error, assuming no clipping?
ask.explanation: Rounding picks the nearest level, so the error is at most half a step: $\Delta/2 = X_m/2^B$ = {{Xm|V}} / {{2^B||6}} = {{Xm/2^B|V}}.

steps.title: Quantization noise
steps.body: For a busy signal the error $e[n]$ looks like noise: uniformly distributed over one step, white, and uncorrelated with the signal. The quantizer then acts as an adder, $\hat{x}[n] = x[n] + e[n]$, and the noise power is the variance of a uniform distribution of width $\Delta$.

steps.prompt: Find the rms quantization noise $\sigma_e$ of a {{B}}-bit converter with a range of $\pm${{Xm|V}} (white-noise model).
The white-noise model describes the quantization error well for a constant (DC) input that sits between two levels.
steps.explanation: For a constant input every sample has the same error: the 'noise' is a constant offset, fully correlated with the signal and not white at all. The model needs a signal that moves across many levels, so that the error looks random from sample to sample. Adding a small random **dither** before the quantizer restores that behaviour.

steps.prompt: One bit is added to an A/D converter with the same full-scale range. What happens to the quantization noise power $\sigma_e^2$?
options: It drops by a factor 4 (−6.02 dB)
It drops by a factor 2 (−3.01 dB)
It does not change; only the range matters
It drops by a factor 16 (−12 dB)
steps.explanation: One more bit doubles the number of levels, so $\Delta$ halves. The noise power goes with $\Delta^2$: a factor 4, or $10\log_{10}4$ = 6.02 dB. That is where '6 dB per bit' comes from.

steps.title: Signal-to-quantization-noise ratio
steps.body: Compare the signal power with $\sigma_e^2 = \Delta^2/12$. For a sine that just fills the range ($\sigma_x^2 = X_m^2/2$) the ratio depends only on the number of bits: $\sigma_x^2/\sigma_e^2 = 1.5 \cdot 2^{2B}$. Each bit halves $\Delta$ and adds 6.02 dB.

steps.prompt: Find the SQNR of an ideal {{B}}-bit converter for a full-scale sine.
A full-scale sine must be digitized with an SQNR of at least {{S}} dB. How many bits does the converter need?

steps.title: Oversampling
steps.body: The white noise power $\sigma_e^2$ is spread evenly from 0 to $f_s/2$. Sample $M$ times faster than needed ($f_s = 2Mf_B$) and the signal band $0 \ldots f_B$ holds only $1/M$ of it. A digital low-pass filter removes the rest before the rate is reduced again.

steps.prompt: A converter oversamples by $M$ = {{M}} (no noise shaping); a digital filter removes the noise outside the signal band.

ask.prompt: By how many dB does this improve the SQNR?
ask.explanation: Only $1/M$ of the white noise falls in the signal band: $10\log_{10}M$ = 10 log₁₀ {{M}} = {{10*log10(M)|dB}}.

ask.prompt: How many bits of extra resolution is that worth?
ask.explanation: $10\log_{10}M$ = {{10*log10(M)|dB}}, and one bit is worth 6.02 dB: {{10*log10(M)|dB}} / 6.02 = $\tfrac{1}{2}\log_2 M$ = {{log2(M)/2}} bits. A factor 4 in rate buys one bit.

steps.title: Noise shaping
steps.body: A sigma-delta modulator feeds the quantization error back so that it leaves through the high-pass filter $1 - z^{-1}$. Its spectrum becomes $4\sigma_e^2\sin^2(\omega/2)$: tiny near DC, large near $\omega = \pi$. The decimation filter cuts away the high-frequency part. Drag $M$: the noise left in the band shrinks much faster than with plain oversampling.

steps.prompt: A first-order ΣΔ modulator runs at an oversampling ratio $M$ = {{M}}. By how many dB do noise shaping and decimation improve the SQNR, compared with a Nyquist-rate converter that uses the same quantizer?
steps.explanation: The in-band noise is about $\sigma_e^2\pi^2/(3M^3)$, so the gain is $10\log_{10}(3M^3/\pi^2) = 30\log_{10}M - 5.17$ = 30 × {{log10(M)||4}} − 5.17 = {{30*log10(M)-5.17|dB}}. Plain oversampling would give only {{10*log10(M)|dB}}.

steps.prompt: Match each change to the SQNR improvement it gives.
steps.explanation: Plain oversampling: in-band noise $\propto 1/M$, so $10\log_{10}2$ = 3 dB per doubling. An order-$L$ shaping loop makes it $\propto 1/M^{2L+1}$: 9 dB for $L$ = 1 and 15 dB for $L$ = 2. An extra bit halves $\Delta$ and quarters the noise power: 6 dB.

steps.prompt: A {{B}}-bit converter digitizes a sine whose peak is {{L}} dB below full scale (−{{L}} dBFS). What is the SQNR?
steps.explanation: A full-scale sine would give 6.02 × {{B}} + 1.76 = {{6.02*B+1.76|dB}}. The noise floor stays put while the signal power drops by {{L}} dB: SQNR = {{6.02*B+1.76|dB}} − {{L}} = {{6.02*B+1.76-L|dB}}. Headroom costs resolution, dB for dB.

steps.prompt: Tested with a full-scale sine, a converter shows a signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SINAD) of {{S}} dB. What is its effective number of bits (ENOB)?
steps.explanation: Invert the full-scale-sine rule: ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76) / 6.02 = ({{S}} − 1.76) / 6.02 = {{(S-1.76)/6.02}} bits. Noise and distortion of the real converter count as extra quantization noise.

steps.prompt: Plain oversampling (no noise shaping) must add {{k}} bits of resolution to a converter for a signal band of 0 to {{fB|Hz}}.

ask.explanation: Each doubling of $M$ adds 3 dB = ½ bit, so $\tfrac{1}{2}\log_2 M$ = {{k}} gives $M = 4^{ {{k}} }$ = {{4^k}}.

steps.prompt: A D/A converter with a zero-order hold runs at {{fs|Hz}}. How much does the hold change the level of a {{f|Hz|4}} tone? Give the gain in dB (negative for a loss).
steps.explanation: $|H_0|/T = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi f/f_s)}{\pi f/f_s}\right|$ with $f/f_s$ = {{r}}: sin({{pi*r||3}} rad) / {{pi*r||3}} = {{sinc(r)||4}}, i.e. 20 log₁₀ {{sinc(r)||4}} = {{20*log10(sinc(r))|dB}}. The droop grows towards $f_s/2$, where it reaches −3.92 dB.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows the quantization-noise spectrum at the output of a first-order sigma-delta modulator? (Horizontal axis: $\omega$ from 0 to $\pi$.)
steps.explanation: The error leaves through $1 - z^{-1}$, so its spectrum is $\sigma_e^2|1 - e^{-j\omega}|^2 = 4\sigma_e^2\sin^2(\omega/2)$: zero at DC and $4\sigma_e^2$ at $\omega = \pi$. The flat line is a plain quantizer; the curve that peaks at DC would push the noise **into** a low-pass signal band.

steps.prompt: An audio A/D converter (signal band 0 to 20 kHz) samples at {{fs|Hz}}; a digital filter removes everything above 20 kHz afterwards. The anti-aliasing filter is an order-$N$ Butterworth with its −3 dB point at 20 kHz, giving about $20N\log_{10}(f/20\,\text{kHz})$ dB at $f$. Find the smallest $N$ that gives {{A}} dB at the first frequency that would alias into the signal band.
steps.explanation: Frequencies above $f_s - f_B$ = {{fs-20000|Hz}} fold into 0 to 20 kHz. There the filter gives $20N\log_{10}$({{fs-20000|Hz}} / 20 kHz) = {{20*log10(ratio)|dB}} × $N$, which must reach {{A}} dB: $N \ge$ {{N0||3}}, so $N$ = {{ceil(N0)}}.

steps.prompt: A first-order ΣΔ modulator must improve the SQNR by {{X}} dB over a Nyquist-rate converter with the same quantizer. Set the oversampling ratio $M$ (the dashed line is the band edge $\pi/M$).
steps.explanation: $30\log_{10}M - 5.17$ = {{X}} gives $M = 10^{({{X}} + 5.17)/30}$ = {{Mt||3}}; in practice you would round up to a power of 2. Plain oversampling would need $M = 10^{ {{X/10}} }$ for the same gain.

steps.prompt: A first-order ΣΔ audio converter (signal band 0 to 20 kHz) uses a {{B}}-bit internal quantizer and samples at {{fs|Hz}}. Use the linear noise model and a full-scale sine.

ask.prompt: Estimate the SQNR after the decimation filter.
ask.explanation: $M = f_s/(2f_B)$ = {{fs|Hz}} / 40 kHz = {{M}}. The quantizer alone: 6.02 × {{B}} + 1.76 = {{6.02*B+1.76|dB}}. Noise shaping adds $30\log_{10}M - 5.17$ = {{30*log10(M)-5.17|dB}}. Total ≈ {{S|dB}}.

ask.prompt: How many effective bits is that?

steps.prompt: A first-order ΣΔ modulator runs at oversampling ratio $M$ = {{M}}. What oversampling ratio would plain oversampling (no noise shaping) need for the same SQNR gain?
steps.explanation: Equal gains: $10\log_{10}M' = 30\log_{10}M - 5.17 = 10\log_{10}(3M^3/\pi^2)$, so $M' = 3M^3/\pi^2$ = 3 × {{M^3||5}} / 9.87 = {{3*M^3/pi^2||3}}. Noise shaping is what lets audio converters get away with 1-bit to 5-bit quantizers.

steps.prompt: An oversampled A/D converter for a 0 to 20 kHz band samples at {{fs|Hz}}. Its anti-aliasing filter is an order-{{N}} Butterworth with the −3 dB point at 20 kHz (about $20N\log_{10}(f/f_B)$ dB well above $f_B$). How much does it attenuate the lowest frequency that aliases into the signal band?
steps.explanation: The lowest frequency that folds into 0 to 20 kHz is $f_s - f_B$ = {{fs-20000|Hz}}. Attenuation ≈ 20 × {{N}} × log₁₀({{ratio||4}}) = {{20*N*log10(ratio)|dB}}: a simple analog filter is enough when the sampling rate is high.

steps.prompt: In an oversampling converter followed by a digital decimation filter, the analog anti-aliasing filter only has to reach its full attenuation at $f_s - f_B$, not already at $f_s/2$.
steps.explanation: Components between $f_s/2$ and $f_s - f_B$ do alias, but they land between $f_B$ and $f_s/2$: outside the signal band, where the digital filter removes them. Only what folds into $0 \ldots f_B$ does harm, and that starts at $f_s - f_B$.

steps.prompt: After decimation, a converter must reach {{S}} dB SQNR for a full-scale sine using plain oversampling with $M$ = {{M}}. How many bits does its quantizer need?
An audio converter uses a first-order ΣΔ loop at $M$ = 64. Which change improves the in-band SQNR the most?
options: Adding one bit to the internal quantizer
Dropping the loop and oversampling plainly at $M$ = 128
steps.explanation: With first-order shaping the in-band noise falls as $1/M^3$: doubling $M$ gains $30\log_{10}2$ = 9 dB, more than the 6.02 dB of an extra bit. Dropping the noise shaping would be a disaster: plain 128× oversampling gains only $10\log_{10}128$ = 21 dB, against $30\log_{10}64 - 5.17$ = 49 dB with the loop.
